entry: American writer of weird, horror, fantasy, and science fiction. He is best known for the [[Cthulhu|Cthulhu Mythos]], a body of works begun by him and extended by later writers that uses his characters, setting and themes. Born in [[Providence, Rhode Island|Providence]], he spent most of his life in [[New England]], and his stories were largely set in a fictionalized version of it. His fiction rests on cosmicism, the view that humanity is an insignificant part of the cosmos. After marrying Sonia Greene in 1924 he moved to [[New York City]], returning to Providence in 1926. Virtually unknown in his lifetime, he published mainly in pulp magazines such as *Weird Tales*. A scholarly revival began in the 1970s, and he is now regarded as one of the most significant 20th-century writers of supernatural horror fiction. His early political views were conservative, and he held racist views for much of his adult life.

Legendary ancient period in Vietnamese historiography, traditionally dated 2879–258 BC. It began with the rule of Kinh Dương Vương over the kingdom of *Văn Lang* and ended when An Dương Vương conquered the state in 258 BC. The 15th-century chronicle *Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư* placed Kinh Dương Vương as the first Hùng king, an absolute monarch, and gave the capital as Phong Châu in present-day Phú Thọ Province. The chronicle bounded Văn Lang by Ba-Shu (present-day [[Sichuan]]) to the west, Dongting Lake ([[Hunan]]) to the north, the [[South China Sea]] to the east and [[Champa]] to the south. The name is the Sino-Vietnamese pronunciation of characters supposedly meaning a mythical giant bird.

First haseki sultan of the [[Ottoman Empire]] and legal wife of [[Suleiman the Magnificent]]. Presumably born in Ruthenia to an Orthodox family, she was captured by [[Tatars|Crimean Tatars]] during a slave raid and taken to [[Constantinople]]. She rose through the imperial harem to become Suleiman's favorite concubine, and he broke Ottoman tradition by freeing and marrying her. She bore at least six children, including the future sultan Selim II. Her correspondence with Suleiman, which included political information and warnings of uprisings, confirms her role as his most trusted adviser. She also influenced relations with Poland. She patronized major public works, including the Haseki Sultan Complex in [[Istanbul]]. Also known as Roxelana, she is commonly considered the most powerful haseki sultan of the Ottoman Empire.

Extinct eagle of the [[South Island]] of [[New Zealand]]. It was the largest eagle known to have existed, with an estimated weight of 10–18 kilograms, and is commonly accepted to be the *pouākai* of Māori mythology. Its size is seen as an evolutionary response to its main prey, the flightless [[Moa|moa]], some of which weighed up to 200 kilograms. Julius von Haast described it in 1871 as *Harpagornis moorei*; DNA later placed it in the genus *Hieraaetus*, closest to the little eagle. It became extinct around 1445, after the arrival of the Māori, who hunted moa, introduced the Polynesian rat and destroyed forest by fire.

Legal procedure invoking a court's jurisdiction to determine whether a detention is lawful. Enforced through a writ, it is one of the prerogative writs that English courts issued in the monarch's name to control inferior courts and public authorities. At common law the official usually had to prove that a detention was authorized. Although often linked to [[Magna Carta]], its origins predate that charter, in the Assize of Clarendon of 1166 under [[Henry II of England|Henry II]]. The procedure was codified by the Habeas Corpus Act 1679. In wartime the writ has been suspended in some countries, including Britain in 1794 and the United States in 1863.

Main industrial method of making [[Ammonia|ammonia]] from nitrogen and hydrogen. Also called the Haber–Bosch process, it passes the gases over a solid iron catalyst at high pressure and temperature. Most of the ammonia is made into nitrogen fertilizer, directly or as [[Ammonium nitrate|ammonium nitrate]] and [[Urea|urea]]. The German chemists [[Fritz Haber]] and Carl Bosch developed it in the first decade of the 20th century; Haber showed it working in the laboratory in 1909, and Bosch scaled it up for BASF. The first industrial plant opened at Oppau in 1913. During [[World War I|World War I]], Germany used it to make nitric acid for explosives after the [[Blockade|Allied blockade]] cut off imports. Most of the hydrogen comes from [[Natural gas|natural gas]]. In 2018 the process produced about 230 million tonnes of ammonia, but it uses 1–2% of the world's energy and causes about 3% of global [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]] emissions.

Set of resources and environmental conditions in an area that support a species' survival and reproduction. A species' habitat is the physical manifestation of its [[Ecological niche|ecological niche]], and the term is species-specific, unlike environment or vegetation. Physical factors include soil, moisture, temperature and light; biotic factors include food and predators. Habitat generalists thrive in many conditions, while specialists need a narrow set. A parasite's habitat may be its host's body or a single host cell. Habitat types classify whole environments by vegetation and climate, such as [[Forest|forest]], [[Steppe|steppe]], grassland, desert, marsh and pond. Habitats change through volcanic eruptions, earthquakes and tsunamis, or gradually with climate, and humans alter them through [[Deforestation|deforestation]] and river damming.

Composite monarchy ruled by the [[House of Habsburg]] from 1282 to 1918. It began with the acquisition of the Duchy of Austria in 1282 and gained the Netherlands in 1482. Habsburg rulers held the [[Holy Roman Empire]] imperial throne from 1438 to 1806, though its realms were not part of the monarchy. From 1804 it was known as the Austrian Empire, and from 1867 as [[Austria-Hungary]]. It was a union of crowns with only partial shared institutions. It disbanded in late 1918, at the end of [[World War I]].

[[Dog|Akita dog]] known for his loyalty to his owner, Hidesaburō Ueno. Born in mid-November 1923 on a farm near Ōdate, Akita Prefecture, Japan, he was taken to Shibuya, Tokyo, in 1924 as a pet of Ueno, a professor at [[University of Tokyo|Tokyo Imperial University]]. He met Ueno at Shibuya Station each day after his commute home. After Ueno died of a [[Aneurysm|cerebral aneurysm]] at work in May 1925, Hachikō returned to the station almost every day until his death in March 1935, reportedly facing neglect and occasional mistreatment. His story became nationally known in Japan and led [[Helen Keller]] to bring the first Akita to America.

Term for a person who seeks unauthorized access to a computer system or network, or for a skilled programmer. The computing sense developed in student culture at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in the late 1950s and early 1960s. Publicized intrusions and the 1983 film *WarGames* later shifted public use toward unauthorized access. Communities include free-software programmers, hardware hackers, and white hat and black hat hackers, whose aims and legal status vary. In security work, authorization and agreed limits separate professional testing from access without permission.

Deepest region of the ocean, lying within oceanic trenches. It ranges from about 6 to 11 km below sea level. The name refers to [[Hades]], the Greek god of the underworld. The term was first proposed in 1956 for depths below 6,000 m, and about 94% of the zone lies in subduction trenches. Its 46 individual habitats cover less than 0.25% of the seafloor, and most are in the [[Pacific Ocean]]. As of 2020, over 400 species were known from hadal ecosystems, with gigantism in amphipods and dwarfism in [[Nematode|nematodes]].

Saltwater ray-finned fish of the cod family, Gadidae, and the only species in the genus *Melanogrammus*. It is native to the North Atlantic and is an important fishery, especially in northern Europe, where it is sold fresh, frozen and smoked. Smoked varieties include Finnan haddie and Arbroath smokie. The largest stocks are in the [[North Sea]], off the [[Faroe Islands]], off [[Iceland]] and off Norway, and it ranges from the [[Bay of Biscay]] to Spitzbergen and the [[Barents Sea]]. Off North America the main commercially fished stock lies from [[Cape Cod]] to the Grand Banks of Newfoundland. Haddock are most often found at depths of 80 to 200 m. The longest recorded was 94 centimetres (37 inches) and weighed 11 kilograms. A black blotch, the "Devil's thumbprint", gives the genus its name.

First and oldest of the four geologic eons of Earth's history. It began with the planet's formation about 4.6 billion years ago and ended 4.031 billion years ago, the age of the oldest known intact rock formations. The name comes from [[Hades]], reflecting the hellish conditions of a molten early Earth. Hadean rocks are very rare, mostly granular [[Zircon|zircons]] from Jack Hills in [[Western Australia]]. The collision that created the [[Moon]] occurred early in the eon. Early Earth had a thick atmosphere of water vapor, methane and ammonia. The eon was succeeded by the [[Archean]].

God of the dead and of riches in ancient Greek religion and mythology, and king of the underworld. He was the eldest son of the [[Titans|Titans]] Cronus and Rhea. He and his brothers [[Zeus]] and [[Poseidon]] overthrew their father's generation and divided the cosmos by lot: Hades received the underworld, Zeus the sky and Poseidon the sea. Mortals avoided his name and used euphemisms; Roman mythographers merged him with other gods into [[Pluto]], a Latinized form of the Greek title Plouton, meaning "the rich one". His name is generally taken to mean "the unseen one". His abduction of Persephone, daughter of [[Demeter]], explained the seasons, and the three-headed dog [[Cerberus]] guarded the gates of his realm.

Reports of the words, actions and silent approvals of the Islamic prophet [[Muhammad]]. The Arabic word means "report" or "account". Traditions circulated orally in early post-prophetic discussion, and scholars compiled them between the 7th and 10th centuries, organized by authority and then by subject. Each hadith is linked to an isnad, a chain of transmitters. Hadith scholars grade reports as sahih ("authentic"), hasan ("good") or da'if ("weak"). Hadith is the second authority after the [[Quran]], and much of [[Sharia]] is derived from it. [[Sunni Islam|Sunni]] and Shia traditions recognize different corpora, while the Kharijites, the Mu'tazila and some early jurists questioned hadith, and Quranists reject them. Many Western scholars argue that the corpus reflects the legal, theological and political conflicts of the 8th to 10th centuries rather than 7th-century reality.

Global-scale tropical atmospheric circulation in which air rises near the equator and sinks in the subtropics. Named after George Hadley, who in 1735 proposed hemisphere-spanning cells to explain the [[Trade winds|trade winds]]. Air rises near the equator, flows poleward near the tropopause at 12–15 km, descends around 30 degrees latitude and returns equatorward near the surface. Converging air forms the [[Intertropical Convergence Zone]], where the heaviest rains fall, and shifts in it cause [[Monsoon|monsoons]]. The sinking branches suppress rainfall, so many of Earth's deserts lie in the subtropics. Since at least the 1980s the circulation has expanded poleward as a result of climate change, and models project that it will widen and weaken through the 21st century.

Spanish-born [[Roman emperor|Roman emperor]] (r. 117–138). Born in Italica, Hispania Baetica, he married Vibia Sabina, a grandniece of [[Trajan]]. He abandoned Trajan's expansionist policies in Mesopotamia, Assyria, Armenia and parts of Dacia, preferring defensible borders. He visited almost every province and favored building projects, including [[Hadrian's Wall]] across northern Britain from AD 122. In [[Rome]] he rebuilt the Pantheon, and he promoted [[Athens]] as the cultural capital of the empire. After the death of his companion Antinous, Hadrian established a popular cult. He suppressed the Bar Kokhba Revolt late in his reign. Soon after his accession he had four senators executed, which earned him the senate's lasting enmity. In 138 he adopted Antoninus Pius as his successor.

Former Roman defensive fortification across northern England, begun in AD 122 in the reign of [[Hadrian]]. It ran about 73 miles (117.5 km) from Wallsend on the River Tyne to Bowness-on-Solway, with large forts, milecastles and turrets. Almost all its standing masonry was removed in early modern times for local roads and farmhouses. The monk and historian [[Bede]] wrote that it stood 12 feet (3.7 metres) high. It is the largest Roman archaeological feature in Britain and was designated a [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Site in 1987. It lies entirely in England and never formed the border with [[Scotland|Scotland]], though it is sometimes described as such.

Composite subatomic particle made of two or more quarks, bound by the strong nuclear force. The name comes from Greek *hadrós*, "stout, thick", and hadrons are analogous to molecules held together by electromagnetism. Most of the mass of ordinary matter comes from the [[Proton|proton]] and [[Neutron|neutron]], and most of their mass comes from the binding energy of their quarks. Hadrons fall into two families: [[Baryon|baryons]], made of three quarks, and [[Meson|mesons]], made of a quark and an antiquark, such as the [[Pion|pion]]. Exotic hadrons, including tetraquark and pentaquark states, have been identified since 2007. Almost all free hadrons decay, though free protons appear stable. Free neutrons have a half-life of about 611 seconds.

Persian lyric poet and Sufi mystic. He was born in [[Shiraz]], where his tomb in the Musalla Gardens is regularly visited. He took the title Hafez, meaning one who has memorized the [[Quran]], for memorizing it at an early age. His Divān, probably compiled after his death, consists largely of [[Ghazal|ghazals]] on love, wine and taverns, expressing religious ecstasy, freedom from restraint and the exposure of hypocrisy. Persian speakers learn his poems by heart and use them as proverbs, and fāl-e Ḥāfez, divination by opening the book at random, is widespread. Patrons included [[Timur]] at the end of his life. Adaptations and translations of his poems exist in all major languages.

[[Chemical element|Chemical element]] with symbol Hf and atomic number 72, a lustrous, silvery gray transition metal. It chemically resembles [[Zirconium|zirconium]], with which it occurs in minerals and from which it is difficult to separate. Predicted by [[Dmitri Mendeleev]] in 1869, it was identified in 1922 by Dirk Coster and George de Hevesy and named after Hafnia, the Latin name for [[Copenhagen]], where it was discovered. Its large [[Neutron|neutron]] capture cross section makes it useful in [[Nuclear reactor|nuclear reactor]] control rods, though it must be removed from the zirconium alloys used in reactors. Its oxide is used in semiconductor processes for integrated circuits at 45 nanometres and smaller. Pure hafnium is not toxic but is pyrophoric, capable of spontaneous combustion in air.

Eel-shaped jawless marine fish of the class Myxini, known for producing slime. Hagfish are the only known living animals with a skull but no vertebral column, though they have rudimentary vertebrae. They are scavengers and predators with simple eyespots and two pairs of horny teeth. When threatened they exude copious slime from glands in the skin; in seawater it expands to 10,000 times its original size in 0.4 seconds. Its fibers let a captured hagfish tie itself in an overhand knot and scrape the slime away. Hagfish and [[Lamprey|lampreys]] form the only living jawless fish groups and are more closely related to each other than to jawed vertebrates. The oldest known hagfish date from the [[Carboniferous|Late Carboniferous]], about 310 million years ago.

Mosque and former cathedral in [[Istanbul]], Turkey, built as a church for the Byzantine emperor [[Justinian I]]. Completed in AD 537, it was the world's largest interior space and among the first to use a fully pendentive dome. As the cathedral of [[Constantinople]] it was the centre of Eastern Orthodoxy for nearly a thousand years, and its design became the model for Eastern Orthodox church architecture and later Ottoman mosques. In 1054 papal envoy Humbert of Silva Candida delivered an excommunication often considered the start of the [[East–West Schism]]. After the Ottoman conquest in 1453 it became a mosque, with minarets added. It was a museum from 1935 until 2020, when it was reclassified as a mosque, a decision that drew condemnation from [[UNESCO]] and others.

Port city in northern [[Israel|Israel]] on the slopes of Mount Carmel. It is the country's third-largest city, after [[Jerusalem]] and [[Tel Aviv]], with a population of 297,082 in 2024. Home to the [[Baháʼí Faith|Baháʼí]] World Centre, a [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage Site]], it has been ruled by Canaanites, Phoenicians, Romans, Ottomans and the British. By 1945 it had a 55% Jewish majority alongside a 45% Arab minority, but most of its Arab residents fled or were expelled during the 1948 war. It is a major seaport, and Haifa Bay is a centre of [[Petroleum|petroleum]] refining and chemical processing.

Short form of Japanese [[Poetry|poetry]], traditionally of 17 on in a 5, 7, 5 pattern across three phrases. Traditional haiku include a kireji, or cutting word, and a kigo, a seasonal reference. It originated as the opening stanza, or hokku, of linked renga verse and became a standalone poem; the name was given at the end of the 19th century by Masaoka Shiki. [[Matsuo Bashō]] raised the form to literary prominence in the late 17th century, and Zen principles of simplicity influenced it. Haiku in English often appear in three lines and vary widely in following traditional rules. Poems that do not follow the rules are generally classed as senryū.
